answers.text: Simple: one instruction: return exactly three lines, in order -- delivery date, item and quantity, change from original order -- using a fixed template. Label each line (Date / Item & Qty / Change) so it's unambiguous which line is which.
Straight up, structure: submitter, date range, itemised lines (date, amount, category), total -- in that fixed order. The total is the sum of the amount column, stated once at the end, not estimated.
There's an error in this email. The call was on the 14th; the 19th is five days later, not the 'three days out' the email states.
No question -- the 15% delivery growth (54 to 62) checks out fine. The on-time rate is wrong: 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%.
I'd sign off Output 2 -- it shows the source figures and the calculation. Output 1 gives no way to see the €612,000 or €25,100 it's built from.
Simple: I'd send Reply 2 -- it names the order and credit references.

Straight up, 1. No -- that's the customer's delivery address, personal data tied to an identifiable customer. 3. No -- next quarter's pricing is unreleased and competitively sensitive. 4. Yes -- it's already published on our own site, so nothing new is exposed.

Unit pricing and volume discounts are sensitive -- redact the figures before pasting anything in. The confidentiality clause names both companies, which makes it a harder no than a generic clause would be. The delivery schedule on its own is low-risk and fine to paste as-is.
No question -- I'd cross-cast the report's totals against the delivery log itself every week. That happens Friday, right before the report goes to the ops manager.
Step 1 -- extracting the item list and quantities -- is where an error would compound downstream.
